title: Oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons

notes.definition: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons. In a redox reaction one species loses electrons (is oxidised) while another gains them (is reduced), and ionic equations show only the particles that change.
explanation: At Foundation level, oxidation and reduction are defined using oxygen. Higher tier students also need a more general definition based on electrons: oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons. A helpful memory aid is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). The two definitions agree. When magnesium burns, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, each magnesium atom loses two electrons to become Mg²⁺ (oxidation, and it also gains oxygen), and each oxygen atom gains two electrons to become O²⁻ (reduction).

Electrons cannot just disappear, so whenever one species loses electrons another species must gain them. This means oxidation and reduction always happen together in a redox reaction. You can show each process separately with a half equation. For magnesium reacting with copper ions: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ shows oxidation (electrons are on the right, as a product, because they are lost), and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu shows reduction (electrons are on the left, because they are gained).

Metal displacement reactions are redox reactions. When magnesium is added to copper sulfate solution, Mg(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Copper sulfate is made of Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions, and magnesium sulfate of Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions. The sulfate ions are in solution at the start and are still there, unchanged, at the end. Ions that are present but do not take part in the reaction are called spectator ions, and they are left out of the ionic equation.

To write an ionic equation for a displacement reaction: write the full balanced equation; split any soluble ionic compounds (aq) into their ions; cross out the spectator ions that appear unchanged on both sides; write what is left. For magnesium and copper sulfate the ionic equation is Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Check that both atoms and charges balance: here the total charge is 2+ on each side. For zinc and silver nitrate, Zn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s): two silver ions are needed to accept the two electrons lost by one zinc atom.

To identify what is oxidised and what is reduced in any equation, look at the charge on each species before and after. A metal atom that becomes a positive ion has lost electrons, so it is oxidised. A metal ion that becomes a neutral atom has gained electrons, so it is reduced. For non-metals, a halogen molecule such as Cl₂ that becomes Cl⁻ ions has gained electrons (reduced), and halide ions such as Br⁻ that become Br₂ have lost electrons (oxidised), as in Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Always name the species, including its charge, for example 'Cu²⁺ ions are reduced'.
keyFacts: Oxidation is the loss of electrons.
Reduction is the gain of electrons.
OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.
Oxidation and reduction always happen together in a redox reaction.
In an oxidation half equation the electrons are on the right: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.
In a reduction half equation the electrons are on the left: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Spectator ions are ions that are present but unchanged in a reaction; they are left out of ionic equations.
Ionic equation for magnesium and copper sulfate: Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
In metal displacement reactions, the more reactive metal is oxidised and the ion of the less reactive metal is reduced.
Ionic equations must balance for both atoms and charge.

keyTerms.definition: The loss of electrons (also the gain of oxygen).
The gain of electrons (also the loss of oxygen).
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction take place at the same time, with electrons transferred from one species to another.
An equation that shows only the particles (atoms, ions or molecules) that take part in a reaction, leaving out spectator ions.
An ion that is present in the reaction mixture but is not changed by the reaction, such as SO₄²⁻ in a displacement reaction with a sulfate.
An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction, including electrons (e⁻).
A general word for any particle in an equation: an atom, molecule or ion.

workedExamples.title: Writing an ionic equation for a displacement reaction
workedExamples.question: Iron reacts with copper sulfate solution: Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Write the ionic equation and identify the species oxidised and reduced.
steps: Split the aqueous ionic compounds into ions: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + Cu(s).
SO₄²⁻ appears unchanged on both sides, so it is a spectator ion. Cross it out.
Ionic equation: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Charges: 2+ on each side.
Fe → Fe²⁺: iron atoms lose 2 electrons, so iron is oxidised.
Cu²⁺ → Cu: copper ions gain 2 electrons, so Cu²⁺ ions are reduced.
workedExamples.answer: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s); Fe is oxidised, Cu²⁺ is reduced.

workedExamples.title: Balancing an ionic equation by charge
workedExamples.question: Copper reacts with silver nitrate solution to form copper nitrate and silver. Write the ionic equation.
steps: Each copper atom loses 2 electrons (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻), but each silver ion gains only 1 electron (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag).
So two Ag⁺ ions are needed for every Cu atom: Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s).

workedExamples.title: Counting electrons transferred
workedExamples.question: Aluminium reacts with copper ions: 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s). How many electrons are transferred in total, as written?
steps: Each Al atom loses 3 electrons: 2 atoms lose 2 × 3 = 6 electrons.
Each Cu²⁺ ion gains 2 electrons: 3 ions gain 3 × 2 = 6 electrons.
Electrons lost = electrons gained, as they must be.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think reduction means losing something, so a reduced species loses electrons.
misconceptions.right: Reduction is the gain of electrons. The name comes from losing oxygen, but in electron terms a reduced species gains electrons (RIG).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think spectator ions do not exist in the solution because they are not in the ionic equation.
misconceptions.right: Spectator ions are still present in the solution; they are left out of the ionic equation only because they do not change.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say 'copper is reduced' when copper ions become copper atoms.
misconceptions.right: The species reduced is the copper ion, Cu²⁺. Copper atoms are the product of reduction.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often balance ionic equations by atoms only.
misconceptions.right: Ionic equations must also balance for charge. For Zn + Ag⁺ you need 2Ag⁺, so that the total charge is 2+ on each side.

realWorld: Scrap iron is used to displace copper from waste copper sulfate solutions; iron atoms are oxidised and Cu²⁺ ions are reduced.
The thermite reaction between aluminium and iron oxide is a redox reaction used to weld railway lines: aluminium is oxidised to Al³⁺ and Fe³⁺ is reduced to iron.
Batteries and fuel cells work by separating the oxidation and reduction half reactions so that the electrons flow through a wire.
higherTier: This whole subtopic is Higher tier only.
Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons (OIL RIG).
Write ionic equations for displacement reactions, leaving out spectator ions.
Identify in a given reaction, symbol equation or half equation which species are oxidised and which are reduced.
examTips: Write OIL RIG at the top of your answer to make sure you get oxidation and reduction the right way round.
Name the species exactly, with charges: 'Cu²⁺ ions are reduced', 'magnesium atoms are oxidised'.
In half equations, electrons go on the right for oxidation and on the left for reduction.
Always check that an ionic equation balances for charge as well as for atoms.
Only split aqueous (aq) ionic compounds into ions. Solids, liquids, gases and metals stay as they are.
summary: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG).
Redox reactions involve electron transfer from one species to another.
Half equations show the oxidation and reduction parts separately.
Spectator ions do not change and are left out of ionic equations.
In displacement, the more reactive metal atom is oxidised and the less reactive metal ion is reduced.
Ionic equations must balance for atoms and charge.

flashcards.front: Is Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ oxidation or reduction?
Is Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu oxidation or reduction?
In a metal displacement reaction, which species is oxidised?
flashcards.back: The atoms of the more reactive metal.

flashcards.front: In Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, what is reduced?

flashcards.front: Which ions are spectators when zinc reacts with copper sulfate?

questions.question: What is oxidation in terms of electrons?
questions.explanation: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons. Gain of electrons is reduction.

questions.question: What is reduction in terms of electrons?
questions.explanation: Reduction Is Gain of electrons. Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus and are not transferred in chemical reactions.

questions.question:
Which process is shown by this half equation?
Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: The magnesium atom loses two electrons (they appear as a product), so this is oxidation.

questions.question:
Zinc reacts with copper sulfate solution:
Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
Which is the ionic equation?
questions.explanation: Sulfate ions are spectators and are removed. The second option is the reverse reaction, and the last option still includes copper sulfate and sulfate ions.

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with iron sulfate solution:
Mg(s) + FeSO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + Fe(s)
Which is the spectator ion?
questions.explanation: Sulfate ions are in solution at the start and at the end and do not change. Fe²⁺ is turned into Fe atoms, and Mg²⁺ is formed from Mg atoms, so both take part.

questions.question:
Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
Which species is reduced?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ gains two electrons to become Cu, so Cu²⁺ is reduced. Fe loses electrons and is oxidised. Fe²⁺ and Cu are products.

questions.question:
Chlorine reacts with potassium bromide solution:
Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq)
Which species is oxidised?
questions.explanation: Bromide ions lose electrons (2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻), so they are oxidised. Chlorine gains electrons and is reduced. Students often pick Cl₂ because it is the more reactive element, but being reactive here means being reduced.

questions.question: Which half equation is correct?
questions.explanation: A neutral aluminium atom loses 3 electrons to form Al³⁺. Charge check: left 0, right 3+ + 3(1−) = 0. Adding electrons to an atom cannot make it positive.

questions.question:
Copper reacts with silver nitrate solution:
Cu(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2Ag(s)
Which is the correct ionic equation?
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions are spectators. Each Cu atom loses 2 electrons and each Ag⁺ gains 1, so 2Ag⁺ are needed. The first option does not balance for charge (1+ on the left, 2+ on the right).

questions.question: Sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride, which contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Which statement is correct?
options: Sodium atoms gain electrons and are reduced
Chlorine atoms lose electrons and are oxidised
Sodium atoms lose electrons and are oxidised
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium atoms lose electrons and are oxidised
questions.explanation: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ is loss of electrons (oxidation). Chlorine gains electrons to form Cl⁻ and is reduced.

questions.question: How many electrons does one magnesium atom lose when it forms a Mg²⁺ ion?
questions.explanation: The charge of 2+ shows that two electrons have been lost: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.

questions.question:
Zn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)
What is the total number of electrons transferred in this equation as written?
questions.explanation: One Zn atom loses 2 electrons; two Ag⁺ ions each gain 1 electron, so 2 are gained. Electrons lost = electrons gained = 2.

questions.question: In a reaction, iron(III) ions (Fe³⁺) are reduced to iron atoms. How many electrons does each Fe³⁺ ion gain?
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Fe. Three electrons are needed to cancel the 3+ charge and make a neutral atom.

questions.question:
Aluminium reacts with copper(II) ions:
2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s)
Calculate the total number of electrons transferred in this equation as written.
markScheme: 1 mark: each Al loses 3 electrons, so 2 × 3 (or each Cu²⁺ gains 2, so 3 × 2)
questions.explanation: Electrons lost by aluminium: 2 × 3 = 6. Electrons gained by copper ions: 3 × 2 = 6. These must be equal, which is why the equation needs 2Al and 3Cu²⁺.

questions.question: The memory aid OIL RIG is used for redox reactions. State what it stands for.
questions.explanation: OIL RIG refers to electrons: oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons.

questions.question: Write a half equation to show a zinc atom forming a zinc ion, Zn²⁺.
questions.explanation: The atom loses two electrons, which are written as a product. Charge: 0 on the left, 2+ and 2− on the right.

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with zinc sulfate solution:
Mg(s) + ZnSO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + Zn(s)
Write the ionic equation for this reaction, including state symbols.
questions.explanation: SO₄²⁻ ions are spectators and are removed. Magnesium atoms are oxidised and zinc ions are reduced.

questions.question: Explain why sulfate ions are not included in the ionic equation for the reaction between iron and copper sulfate solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: they are spectator ions / they are unchanged in the reaction (present in solution before and after)
questions.explanation: Ionic equations only show species that change. The sulfate ions are in solution at the start and at the end.

questions.question:
Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
Identify the species oxidised and the species reduced. Explain in terms of electrons.
markScheme: 1 mark: Fe (iron atoms) is oxidised because it loses (two) electrons
1 mark: Cu²⁺ (copper ions) is reduced because it gains (two) electrons
questions.explanation: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation) and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction). Naming 'copper' rather than 'copper ions' for the reduced species would not get the mark.

questions.question: Explain why metal displacement reactions are described as redox reactions.
markScheme: 1 mark: the (more reactive) metal atoms lose electrons / are oxidised
1 mark: the ions of the less reactive metal gain electrons / are reduced (so oxidation and reduction happen together)
questions.explanation: Electrons are transferred from the more reactive metal to the ions of the less reactive metal. One loses, one gains, so both oxidation and reduction occur.

questions.question: Zinc reacts with silver nitrate solution, AgNO₃(aq), to form zinc nitrate solution and silver. Write the balanced ionic equation, including state symbols.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct species Zn + Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Ag
1 mark: balanced with 2Ag⁺ and 2Ag and correct state symbols
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions are spectators. Zinc loses 2 electrons but each Ag⁺ gains only 1, so two silver ions are needed. Charge: 2+ on each side.

questions.question:
Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
State whether the lead ion is oxidised or reduced in this half equation.
questions.explanation: Electrons are on the left side, so the Pb²⁺ ion gains them. Gain of electrons is reduction.

questions.question:
A piece of magnesium ribbon is placed in blue copper sulfate solution. After some time, a brown solid forms on the magnesium and the blue colour fades.
Explain these observations. In your answer include the full balanced equation, the ionic equation and half equations, and identify what is oxidised and what is reduced in terms of electrons.
markScheme: Indicative content: magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper; brown solid is copper; blue colour fades because Cu²⁺ ions (which make the solution blue) are used up and replaced by colourless Mg²⁺ ions; full equation Mg(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + Cu(s); sulfate ions are spectator ions; ionic equation Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s); half equations Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; magnesium atoms lose electrons so are oxidised; copper ions gain electrons so are reduced; redox reaction.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): observations fully explained, correct full and ionic equations, correct half equations, oxidation and reduction correctly identified in terms of electrons with species named precisely.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): displacement explained with a correct equation and correct identification of oxidation and reduction, with some errors or omissions in the ionic or half equations.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example magnesium is more reactive than copper, or copper is formed, with little correct use of electrons.
questions.explanation: The colour change and brown solid are explained by Cu²⁺ ions becoming copper atoms. The electron transfer is from Mg atoms to Cu²⁺ ions; sulfate is a spectator.

questions.question:
In the thermite reaction, aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide:
2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe
Aluminium oxide contains Al³⁺ ions and iron(III) oxide contains Fe³⁺ ions.
Explain why this is a redox reaction, using both the oxygen definition and the electron definition. Include half equations.
markScheme: Indicative content: oxygen definition: aluminium gains oxygen so it is oxidised; iron oxide loses oxygen so it is reduced; electron definition: aluminium atoms lose 3 electrons each, Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻, so aluminium is oxidised; Fe³⁺ ions gain 3 electrons each, Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Fe, so iron(III) ions are reduced; oxide ions are unchanged; both definitions agree; oxidation and reduction happen together, so it is redox.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both definitions applied correctly with correct half equations and correct identification of species oxidised and reduced.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one definition applied correctly, or oxidised and reduced species identified with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The oxide ions (O²⁻) do not change, so in electron terms they are spectators. Electrons pass from Al atoms to Fe³⁺ ions.

questions.question:
Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Magnesium oxide is made of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions.
Compare the oxygen and electron definitions of oxidation and reduction, using this reaction as an example.
markScheme: Indicative content: oxygen definition: oxidation is gain of oxygen, reduction is loss of oxygen; magnesium gains oxygen so is oxidised; electron definition: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons; each Mg atom loses 2 electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻) so magnesium is oxidised; each oxygen atom gains 2 electrons (O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻) so oxygen is reduced; the oxygen definition cannot describe what happens to oxygen itself, but the electron definition can; both definitions agree that magnesium is oxidised.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both definitions stated and applied correctly to magnesium and oxygen, with a clear comparison.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): definitions stated with limited application to the reaction.
questions.explanation: The electron definition is more general: it works for reactions with no oxygen (such as displacement in solution) and shows that oxygen is reduced when a metal burns.

questions.question: In the half equation 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻, the chloride ions are:
markScheme: 1 mark: oxidised, because they lose electrons
questions.explanation: Electrons appear as a product, so the chloride ions have lost them. Loss of electrons is oxidation.

questions.question:
Iron reacts with chlorine: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. Iron(III) chloride contains Fe³⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
Write the two half equations for this reaction and identify the species oxidised.
questions.explanation: Iron atoms lose three electrons each; each chlorine molecule gains two electrons to form two chloride ions. 2Fe lose 6 electrons and 3Cl₂ gain 6, so electrons balance.
